Let

\[
S=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\sum_{j=1}^{100}2^{-\lfloor 101k/j\rfloor}.
\]

For fixed \(j\), we have

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{101(k+j)}{j}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor \frac{101k}{j}+101\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor \frac{101k}{j}\right\rfloor+101,
\]

so

\[
2^{-\lfloor 101(k+j)/j\rfloor}=2^{-101}\,2^{-\lfloor 101k/j\rfloor}.
\]

Thus the terms for fixed \(j\) repeat every \(j\) with a factor \(2^{-101}\), giving

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}2^{-\lfloor 101k/j\rfloor}
=
\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{j}2^{-\lfloor 101t/j\rfloor}}{1-2^{-101}}.
\]

Hence

\[
S=\frac{1}{1-2^{-101}}
\sum_{j=1}^{100}\sum_{t=1}^{j}2^{-\lfloor 101t/j\rfloor}.
\]

Now evaluate the finite double sum. For \(m=1,\dots,101\), let \(C_m\) be the number of pairs \((j,t)\) with \(1\le j\le 100\), \(1\le t\le j\), and \(\lfloor 101t/j\rfloor=m\).

- For \(m=101\), we must have \(t=j\), so \(C_{101}=100\).
- For \(m=100\), the condition gives \(100j/101\le t<j\), which is impossible, so \(C_{100}=0\).
- For \(1\le m\le 99\), the condition is

\[
\frac{mj}{101}\le t<\frac{(m+1)j}{101}.
\]

Since \(101\) is prime, both endpoints are non-integers, so for fixed \(j\) the number of integers \(t\) is

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{(m+1)j}{101}\right\rfloor-
\left\lfloor \frac{mj}{101}\right\rfloor.
\]

Thus

\[
C_m=\sum_{j=1}^{100}
\left(
\left\lfloor \frac{(m+1)j}{101}\right\rfloor-
\left\lfloor \frac{mj}{101}\right\rfloor
\right).
\]

Using

\[
\sum_{j=1}^{100}\left\lfloor \frac{aj}{101}\right\rfloor=50(a-1)
\qquad(1\le a\le 100),
\]

we get

\[
C_m=50m-50(m-1)=50
\]

for \(1\le m\le 99\).

Therefore

\[
\sum_{j=1}^{100}\sum_{t=1}^{j}2^{-\lfloor 101t/j\rfloor}
=
50\sum_{m=1}^{99}2^{-m}+100\cdot 2^{-101}.
\]

Since \(\sum_{m=1}^{99}2^{-m}=1-2^{-99}\), this equals

\[
50(1-2^{-99})+100\cdot 2^{-101}
=
\frac{100(2^{100}-1)}{2^{101}}.
\]

Finally,

\[
S=
\frac{1}{1-2^{-101}}\cdot
\frac{100(2^{100}-1)}{2^{101}}
=
\frac{100(2^{100}-1)}{2^{101}-1}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac{100(2^{100}-1)}{2^{101}-1}}
\]
